headings: Task 3 - A Scenic 101 km Race Through Baixo Guandu
pwca_news~521b9ec104.normalized_text:
back to all news
Task 3 - A Scenic 101 km Race Through Baixo Guandu
07/10/2026
Task 3 of the Paragliding World Cup in Brazil took pilots on a 101 km course through some less frequently used areas around Baixo Guandu.
From the main takeoff, the task first headed south — a direction rarely used during competition — before turning northwest and eventually east, crossing over the famous “whale” on the way towards goal at the airport.
The southern part of the course offered some spectacular scenery, and the conditions provided a perfect opportunity for the pilots to explore this part of the flying area.
Throughout most of the task, the leading group remained very compact. Positions changed constantly, with different pilots taking turns at the front and very little separating the main contenders.
On the final leg, Andy Aebi found himself in front and crossed the End of Speed Section with the fastest time. However, once leading points were taken into account, it was Carlos Avila who came out on top. His time spent leading the race earned him the largest share of leading points and ultimately secured the task victory.
The finish was extremely close, with most pilots arriving within just five minutes of the first finisher.
In the end, Task 3 delivered a fast, tightly fought and incredibly scenic race — a perfect demonstration of what makes flying and competing in Baixo Guandu so special.

headings: A Strong Start to the PWC in Brazil
pwca_news~6715b9c038.normalized_text:
back to all news
A Strong Start to the PWC in Brazil
03/10/2026
The Paragliding World Cup in Brazil is underway, with the first two tasks delivering very different but highly competitive races.
Task 1 was flown under mostly cloudy skies, with only occasional periods of sunshine. The conditions were not particularly easy, but remained workable throughout the day, and the task setting matched them well with good timing and an appropriate distance.
The opening leg into wind proved challenging before the race opened up into a long, fast section where pilots could make good progress. The final part towards goal was expected to offer some of the best conditions of the day, but reality turned out differently. Extensive shading made the climbs weaker and more difficult, slowing the race considerably.
The closing kilometres became increasingly demanding, with many pilots landing before the End of Speed Section and several others between ESS and goal. Despite the challenging finish, it was a well-balanced and competitive first task, completed without any accidents.
Task 2 brought an 85 km race and some interesting tactical decisions right from the start. Early on, the leading group stayed higher and followed a line closer to the mountains, while another group pushed farther out into the flats. The flatter route proved to be the better choice and allowed those pilots to move into the front of the race.
According to Tim Bollinger, the section through the volcano became one of the trickiest parts of the task. He initially tried to push ahead alone, but the difficult-to-read lines allowed several groups to regroup and the race came back together.
From there, conditions improved, with good thermals and fast racing towards the final turnpoint. Tim Bollinger and Andy Aebi were among the pilots pushing at the front, but after turning towards ESS they found a less favourable line and had to stop for another climb.
Meanwhile, the eventual task winner found a much stronger line farther to the right. Despite being lower initially, he was able to continue almost directly through the final section, reaching the last turnpoint and goal without needing another climb.
After the first two tasks, Andy Aebi leads the overall ranking, while Violeta Jimenez is leading the women’s classification. Ozone currently leads the team ranking.
Two very different tasks have already tested both patience and tactical decision-making, making for a strong and competitive opening to the World Cup in Brazil.

headings: A Tactical Final Day in Baixo Guandu
pwca_news~82eb01c33a.normalized_text:
back to all news
A Tactical Final Day in Baixo Guandu
10/10/2026
The final task of the PWC Brazil was flown in weaker conditions, making it a noticeably slower and more tactical race under another mostly blue sky.
The first part of the course stayed close to take-off, where several local government officials were visiting. It created a rare opportunity to watch the race unfold live in front of the launch while comparing the action in the sky with the live tracking shown on a large screen provided by the organizers.
The difficult conditions quickly broke the field into smaller groups, and that pattern remained throughout most of the task. Any pilot who pushed too far ahead of the main groups took a significant risk, with several paying the price and going “prego” — the Brazilian term for bombing out.
In the end, 26 pilots reached goal, with two pilots crossing the End of Speed Section in exactly the same second.
The overall task win went to Julien Wirtz, while Violeta Jimenez took the win in the female category.
At the top of the overall rankings, Andy Aebi held onto the lead and secured the competition victory after an exceptionally consistent week of racing. His performance also brought back memories of the 2005 World Championship in Governador Valadares, where he showed the same kind of consistency to achieve another major result in Brazil.
A fitting end to a competitive week in Baixo Guandu, with six tasks showcasing everything from fast racing to difficult tactical decisions and dramatic finishes.

headings: A Dramatic Finish in Unusual Baixo Guandu Conditions
pwca_news~84223181d6.normalized_text:
back to all news
A Dramatic Finish in Unusual Baixo Guandu Conditions
08/10/2026
Task 4 brought some rather unusual conditions for Baixo Guandu, with blue skies, scattered cirrus clouds and noticeably lower thermal tops. An inversion around 1,800 metres AMSL limited the available altitude, but despite this, the race still progressed at a decent pace.
For much of the task, the field remained relatively compact, with most pilots able to stay together until the later stages of the race.
During the southbound leg, however, two distinct groups began to form. The separation between them gradually increased as the task progressed, setting up a very different final phase for each group.
The real drama came on the last leg towards goal, which was flown against the wind. The first group reached the End of Speed Section, and those who still had enough altitude were able to continue directly to goal.
For the rest, the situation became much more difficult. With the conditions weakening and the wind increasing, gaining the necessary altitude became increasingly challenging. Many pilots were unable to climb enough to complete the final push to goal, and the second group eventually faced the same problem.
In the end, only five pilots made goal, while 25 pilots finished between ESS and goal.
It was a difficult task, but still extremely competitive — and with such a dramatic final leg, a particularly exciting one to follow from the ground.

headings: A 56 km Race Decided by the Final Valley Crossing
pwca_news~85965d3e18.normalized_text:
back to all news
A 56 km Race Decided by the Final Valley Crossing
12/09/2026
Yesterday brought Task 4, a 56 km race that would ultimately become the final task of the competition.
The course had initially been planned slightly longer, but with the atmosphere proving more stable than expected, the task was shortened before launch. As on Task 3, the route was designed as a zigzag between the mountains and the flats, allowing pilots to make use of the stronger climbs over the higher terrain while crossing the more stable sections further out in the valley.
Before the start, pilots once again positioned themselves deep in the mountains, climbing as high as possible while waiting for the start gate to open. Some reached almost 3,000 metres. Although the start cylinder itself was around seven kilometres out in front of the mountains, the extra altitude made this the most advantageous place to begin the race.
When the gate opened, the field glided out towards the start before taking the first turnpoint in the flats and returning towards the mountains for the second. From there, enough altitude remained for many pilots to continue directly back out to the third turnpoint in the flats without needing another climb.
Back in the mountains, however, another climb was needed before reaching the fourth turnpoint, which sat higher in the terrain. The course then headed further out into the flats on a longer glide, and this became one of the first difficult sections of the day. The more stable air offered fewer reliable climbs than the mountains, forcing pilots to search around the smaller hills between the ridge and the turnpoint. Several pilots were unable to reconnect and landed here.
Those who made it back to the mountains climbed again before completing another short excursion into the flats and returning once more to the ridge.
The decisive part of the task came before the final major valley crossing. Pilots needed to gain as much altitude as possible before committing to the long glide towards the final turnpoint and the end of speed section. Two main groups formed in different climbing areas along the mountain, eventually reaching similar altitudes before setting off across the valley.
From there, every metre mattered.
The lower pilots began to struggle before reaching the end of speed section. With very little lift available across the valley, some were forced to stop and search for a climb, while others landed short altogether.
For those who arrived with just enough altitude, however, the situation changed completely. A strong thermal was working almost directly on the end-of-speed line, meaning that pilots reaching it with even around 100 metres of height — or less — were able to connect with the climb and continue safely towards goal.
That final crossing proved to be the defining challenge of Task 4.
Noé Court took the task win after arriving ahead of much of the main group, while Keiko Hiraki once again won the women’s category, completing a remarkable run of task victories throughout the competition.
With thunderstorms forecast for the final day, further flying was cancelled, making Task 4 the last race of the event.
That leaves Stanislav Klikar as the overall winner of the competition, Keiko Hiraki as the women’s winner, and Sky Paragliders as the winning team.
pwca_news~85965d3e18.title: Paragliding World Cup

headings: Racing Under Blue Skies
pwca_news~a56a7aff45.normalized_text:
back to all news
Racing Under Blue Skies
09/10/2026
After the drama of the previous day’s final leg, Task 5 brought a smoother race through Baixo Guandu, despite similarly challenging conditions.
The sky was again mostly blue, with a lower cloud base and reduced thermal tops, but this time the route avoided the difficult final leg against the wind and used a finish better suited to the stronger northerly and north-easterly flow.
The task worked well, with a large number of pilots making goal and only around five or six finishing between the End of Speed Section and goal.
The route followed a similar direction to the previous task, giving the pilots another competitive race through the same area under slightly different circumstances.
Overall, it was a solid task with a high goal rate and a much easier final section than the day before.

headings: PWC Baixo Guandu: Back to Brazil
pwca_news~d979e5e1c1.normalized_text:
back to all news
PWC Baixo Guandu: Back to Brazil
29/09/2026
The Paragliding World Cup heads to Brazil for the third event of the 2026 season, following Gemona in Italy and Sopot in Bulgaria. The competition returns to Baixo Guandu, a well-known flying area in Espírito Santo, where the mix of flatland, hills and low mountains offers plenty of options for task setting.
The Flying Place
Baixo Guandu is located in the centre-west of Espírito Santo, around 186 km from the state capital, Vitória. The flying area covers a mix of flatland, rolling hills and low mountains, allowing for a variety of cross-country routes.
To the north, the flying area extends towards Pancas, known for its large granite formations and the Pontões Capixabas Natural Monument, also known as “Jurassic Park”.
Flying Conditions
Thermals in Baixo Guandu are usually strong and consistent and are often marked by clouds. The combination of relatively good climbs and varied terrain puts the emphasis on route choice and efficient transitions.
Pilots can expect different options throughout the day, with the best routes often depending on where the next reliable climb can be found.
The Competition
Baixo Guandu has hosted World Cup competitions before and is a familiar venue on the international calendar. After the first two events of the 2026 season in Gemona and Sopot, the competition now moves to a very different type of flying in Brazil.
With varied terrain and relatively moderate thermals, Baixo Guandu should make for a technical week of racing, where finding the right route and staying efficient through the transitions will be important.
Daily reports, results, photos, and video highlights will be published throughout the event on the official Paragliding World Cup channels
